subtopicTitle: Inner product spaces — dot product generalization

cards.front: Define an inner product on a real vector space V.
cards.back: A function $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle: V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ that is bilinear, symmetric ($\langle u,v \rangle = \langle v,u \rangle$), and positive definite ($\langle v,v \rangle \ge 0$ with equality iff $v=0$).

cards.front: How is the Euclidean dot product a special case of an inner product?
cards.back: On $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\langle x,y \rangle = x^T y = \sum x_i y_i$ satisfies bilinearity, symmetry, and positive-definiteness, hence is an inner product.

cards.front: State the three axioms an inner product must satisfy over $\mathbb{C}$.
cards.back:
1. Linearity in first argument: $\langle au+bv,w \rangle = a\langle u,w \rangle + b\langle v,w \rangle$.
2. Conjugate symmetry: $\langle u,v \rangle = \overline{\langle v,u \rangle}$.
3. Positive-definiteness: $\langle v,v \rangle > 0$ for $v \ne 0$.

cards.front: Define the norm induced by an inner product.
cards.back: $\|v\| = \sqrt{\langle v,v \rangle}$. It satisfies the norm axioms; the inner-product norm is the unique norm compatible with the inner product via the polarization identity.

cards.front: Give the inner product on the space of continuous functions $C[a,b]$.
cards.back: $\langle f,g \rangle = \int_a^b f(x)g(x)\,dx$. It is bilinear, symmetric, and positive definite on the quotient space modulo functions that vanish almost everywhere.

cards.front: Define orthogonality and an orthonormal set in an inner product space.
cards.back: Vectors $u,v$ are orthogonal if $\langle u,v \rangle = 0$. A set $\{e_i\}$ is orthonormal if $\langle e_i,e_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}$.

cards.front: State the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and when equality holds.
cards.back: $|\langle u,v \rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|$, with equality iff $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent.

cards.front: Write the polarization identity that recovers the inner product from the norm (real case).
